query: Which material can be used for superconducting properties, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A refractory high‐entropy alloy (HEA) designed with a substantial fraction of traditional superconducting elements such as Nb (niobium) and Ti (titanium) can exhibit superconducting properties at cryogenic temperatures because Nb and Ti are known to support electron–phonon coupling conducive to Cooper pair formation.
generation.material_initial_state: A cast, homogeneous refractory HEA with near-equiatomic composition including Nb, Ti, and other refractory elements (e.g., Ta, Zr) presenting a stable BCC (or single‐phase) microstructure at ambient temperature.
generation.intervention: Synthesize the NbTi-containing refractory HEA and then subject the material to cryogenic cooling.
generation.conditions: Cooling under cryogenic conditions (using a liquid helium environment) to temperatures below approximately 20 K, while maintaining a controlled, low-defect microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: The single-phase BCC microstructure, which minimizes scattering from grain boundaries and impurities, is anticipated to mediate coherent electron transport.
generation.mechanism: Electron–phonon coupling in the Nb/Ti-rich alloy is hypothesized to lead to the formation of Cooper pairs once the critical temperature is reached, resulting in superconductivity (i.e. zero electrical resistance and the expulsion of magnetic fields via the Meissner effect).
generation.predicted_outcome: Below a certain critical temperature (Tc), the alloy should exhibit a transition to zero electrical resistance and a measurable Meissner effect, indicating superconductivity.
generation.baseline: At ambient temperature, the alloy behaves as a normal metal with finite electrical resistance and standard magnetic susceptibility.
generation.boundary: Superconductivity is expected only if the alloy retains its homogeneous single-phase microstructure with minimal defects; deviations or secondary phases may inhibit or suppress superconducting behavior.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the optimal composition ratio, the precise critical temperature, and whether the multi-element, high-entropy design may introduce disorder that either supports or disrupts the conventional electron–phonon coupling mechanisms seen in simpler superconductors.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of the NbTi-containing refractory HEA with controlled processing conditions to ensure a single-phase microstructure. Cool the samples in a cryogenic setup (such as a liquid helium cryostat) and concurrently measure the electrical resistance and magnetic susceptibility as a function of temperature.
measurements: Temperature-dependent electrical resistance (looking for a drop to zero resistance)
Magnetic susceptibility via SQUID magnetometry (to detect the onset of the Meissner effect)
Determination of the superconducting critical temperature (Tc)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, upon cooling, the material does not exhibit a sudden transition to zero electrical resistance and the expected expulsion of magnetic flux (Meissner effect) below a specific temperature (e.g., 20 K or lower), then the hypothesis that the designed HEA exhibits superconductivity is falsified.
